section_summary: This section documents Japan’s wartime plans to build a self-sufficient Japan–Manchukuo–China economic bloc and a broader Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere. Embassy, military, and naval reports examine the bloc’s industrial, agricultural, financial, labor, trade, transport, and resource policies, including North China production targets and Japanese investments across Southeast Asia. Other documents report shortages in Japan’s staple-fibre industry and the contested, slow implementation of the domestic “New Economic Structure,” which sought greater state direction while retaining limited private management.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of telegram no. 489 concerning the North China five-year plan
subfiles.about: The Embassy evaluates the announced North China five-year plan as a continuation and strengthening of Japanese economic-control policies.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy finds no evidence that Japan has recognized the excessive optimism or failures of its earlier economic plans. Despite occasional concessions to Chinese and commercial interests, Japanese-occupied areas remain subject to restrictive state control designed chiefly to benefit Japan. The North China five-year plan and Tokyo’s yen-bloc program are therefore interpreted as efforts to reinforce existing policy.

subfiles.title: Confidential duplicate paraphrase of telegram no. 489
subfiles.about: This duplicate copy repeats the Embassy’s assessment of Japanese plans for North China and the yen bloc.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports that Japanese publicity offers no sign of a fundamental change in economic policy or an admission that earlier schemes were unrealistic. It concludes that persistent restrictions and state control indicate an intention to intensify Japan’s exploitation of China, especially North China and Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Potential economic pressure on Japan by the United States and Great Britain
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a memorandum about a Japanese Foreign Ministry warning concerning possible Anglo-American economic pressure.
subfiles.summary: The referenced memorandum described a warning sent by the Japanese Foreign Ministry to Japanese representatives in Central and South America during October 1940. The original was filed elsewhere under file number 894.20210/71.

subfiles.title: Japanese economic mission
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram reporting the return of a Japanese economic mission after talks with the Governor General of French Indochina.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese mission was returning home after more than a month of discussions with the Governor General. The report indicated that the mission had obtained less than it sought.

subfiles.title: Economic negotiations between Japan and Indochina
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram about a Nichi Nichi editorial criticizing delays in Japan–Indochina negotiations.
subfiles.summary: The editorial argued that the Japanese and Indochinese positions differed fundamentally and that the talks were not ordinary commercial negotiations. It urged Japan to take a more aggressive diplomatic stance toward the Netherlands Indies to facilitate acceptance of Japanese demands.

subfiles.title: Brief internal comment on the economic plan
subfiles.about: An internal handwritten comment characterizes the plan as grandiose but containing little that is new.
subfiles.summary: The reviewer recommends that the plan be noted briefly. The principal judgment is that, despite its grand scale, it adds little or nothing substantively new.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 5200: Plan for Economic Construction of Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits and evaluates an official account of Japan’s ten-year plan for the Japan–Manchukuo–China bloc.
subfiles.summary: Grew finds no indication that Japanese planners consider earlier yen-bloc schemes overly optimistic. He describes the new program as an intensified assertion of permanent Japanese dominance in the Far East, intended to rationalize industry, finance, and commerce for maximum production and defense. Although foreigners might dismiss it as grandiose, Grew warns that Japanese policymakers regard it as vital and worth risking the nation’s destiny to achieve.

subfiles.title: Summary of the Program for Economic Construction Embracing Japan, “Manchukuo” and China
subfiles.doc_type: official program reproduced as an enclosure
subfiles.about: The official statement sets out the purposes, principles, and sectoral policies of Japan’s ten-year economic-bloc program.
subfiles.summary: The program calls for a self-supporting Japan–Manchukuo–China economy under Japanese leadership and its eventual extension across Greater East Asia. It assigns industrial, agricultural, and labor roles to each territory, promotes Japanese settlement in Manchuria, and proposes planned capital allocation, payments arrangements, productive trade, and integrated transportation. The intended result is reduced dependence on outside powers, increased defense capacity, and a new regional economic order within approximately ten years.

subfiles.title: Departmental abstract of despatch no. 5245
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes Tokyo’s report on North China’s agricultural role under the ten-year plan.
subfiles.summary: The enclosed press report proposed making North China independent of foreign cotton while expanding cereal output. It also described plans for a North China Farm Land Development Company capitalized at thirty million yen.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 5245: Japanese Program for Agricultural Production in North China
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits a press report outlining North China’s agricultural assignments under the ten-year economic plan.
subfiles.summary: North China was expected to increase cotton, wheat, millet, kaoliang, and corn production so the economic bloc could reduce its dependence on the United States and other foreign suppliers. The plan aimed to raise raw-cotton production to ten million piculs and wheat output from 132 million to 147 million piculs by 1950. Grew also notes the envisioned transfer of Japan’s textile industry to China, especially North China.

subfiles.title: North China Now Ready to Increase Cotton
subfiles.from: Domei / The Japan Times and Advertiser
subfiles.about: The article details production targets and land-development measures for North China’s cotton and cereal program.
subfiles.summary: The plan sought near agricultural self-sufficiency and a large regional supply of cotton by 1950, with specified increases in wheat, millet, kaoliang, corn, and rice. A proposed North China Farm Land Development Company would use Japanese techniques to reclaim alkali flats and other waste land, creating 85,000 hectares of rice paddies and roughly 480,000 hectares of dry farms within five years.

subfiles.title: Departmental digest of despatch no. 5284
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes Takahashi’s defense of the East Asiatic Co-Prosperity Sphere and the Embassy’s criticism of it.
subfiles.summary: Takahashi accused Britain and the United States of keeping East Asia dependent by encouraging export raw materials while obstructing independent industrial development. He presented the Co-Prosperity Sphere as the region’s means of emancipation. The Embassy observed that Japan intended to practice the same exploitation it condemned but that the argument would appeal to Japanese audiences seeking a foreign scapegoat.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 5284: East Asiatic Co-Prosperity Sphere
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The despatch digests and critiques Takahashi’s economic justification for the East Asiatic Co-Prosperity Sphere.
subfiles.summary: Takahashi claimed that Britain and the United States had deliberately subordinated East Asia by controlling resource development, industry, trade, communications, labor policy, and banking. He argued that East Asia should develop heavy industry and technical capacity, integrate its resources and markets, and become an autonomous economic unit. The Embassy rejected the argument as untenable for Japan, stressed Japan’s lack of resources and imperial record, and concluded that Japanese success would require both displacing Western interests and obtaining cooperation from other Asian peoples.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting a memorandum on Japan’s material resources
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle, Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hoover transmits a photostatic copy of a memorandum concerning Japan’s material resources.
subfiles.summary: The covering letter forwards recently obtained information on Japanese material resources. Copies were also directed to Naval Intelligence and the War Department’s G-2 office.

subfiles.title: Japan: Material Resources—Staple Fibre
subfiles.about: The memorandum assesses Japan’s staple-fibre production, inputs, quality problems, and wartime shortages.
subfiles.summary: Japan promoted staple fibre as a national substitute for restricted cotton, but production fell sharply from its March 1938 level because of shortages of pulp, labor, power, and coal. The memorandum supplies monthly output figures for 1939 and the first half of 1940 and lists the chemical and coal requirements for producing one ton. It also reports poor-quality fabrics and shoes whose fibre weakened when wet.

subfiles.title: Criticism of the New Economic Structure and Imperial Rule Assistance Association
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram reporting Akaike’s criticism of the government’s economic and political organizations.
subfiles.summary: The referenced telegram concerned alleged failure and communist elements in the New Economic Structure and dissatisfaction with the Imperial Rule Assistance Association. The criticism came from Akaike, a member of the House of Peers.

subfiles.title: Departmental note on Naval Intelligence report no. 180
subfiles.about: The note describes a Naval Intelligence report on Japanese economic activity in the South Seas.
subfiles.summary: The cited report reproduces an Asahi Weekly survey of the natural and economic resources of the South Seas region. It also identifies Japanese companies involved in developing resources in particular territories.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence report no. 180: Japanese Economic Activities in the South Seas Area
subfiles.from: H. H. Smith-Hutton, Naval Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Intelligence Division, Office of the Chief of Naval Operations
subfiles.about: The report surveys Japan’s Southward Advance and its mining, plantation, forestry, and fishing interests across Southeast Asia and the western Pacific.
subfiles.summary: The report estimates Japanese investment in the South Seas at ¥250 million and argues that Japan was combining military and economic steps to secure and consolidate regional holdings. It describes negotiations with French Indochina and the Netherlands Indies, as well as bases bringing Japan within range of Malaya, Borneo, and Java. Drawing on Soji Okada’s Asahi Weekly article, it catalogs Japanese interests in petroleum, tin, iron, nickel, bauxite, precious metals, rubber, hemp, forestry, and fisheries throughout the region.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence report no. 189: Greater East Asia Economic Policy—A Ten Year Plan
subfiles.from: H. H. Smith-Hutton, Naval Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Office of the Chief of Naval Operations
subfiles.about: The report reproduces the Japanese Cabinet’s main lines for a ten-year Japan–Manchukuo–China economic bloc.
subfiles.summary: The plan seeks national economic reorganization, consolidation of the three-country economy, and creation of an East Asian sphere of common prosperity. It calls for regional self-sufficiency and assigns complementary industrial, agricultural, and labor functions to Japan, Manchukuo, and China. Japan would direct heavy industry, technical training, settlement, and resource development, while broader measures would regulate finance, trade, and communications.

subfiles.title: Departmental comparison of military and naval reports on the Ten-Year Plan
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes two intelligence reports reproducing the Cabinet Information Bureau’s ten-year plan.
subfiles.summary: Both reports identify three objectives: reorganizing Japan’s national economy, firmly organizing the Japan–Manchukuo–China economy, and establishing an East Asian common-prosperity sphere. Six enumerated policies would regulate industry, labor, finance, communications, and trade in order to achieve self-sufficiency and strengthen the bloc’s world economic position.

subfiles.title: Military Attaché report no. 10,234: Ten-Year Plan for Japan, China and Manchukuo
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Cresswell, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The report translates the official ten-year economic plan and comments on its mechanisms and prospects.
subfiles.summary: The translated program proposes a self-sufficient regional unit directed by Japan, with planned roles for industry, agriculture, labor, finance, trade, and communications. It calls for heavy and precision industry in Japan, mining and power development in Manchukuo, resource and industrial expansion in China, transfers of light industry to the continent, and integrated capital and payments systems. Cresswell judges it the clearest statement yet of the bloc project but notes that success depends on the China war, cooperation from occupied territories, and the outcome of the war in Europe. If successful, he concludes, the resulting Oriental economic bloc would be powerful and substantially independent of outside supplies.

subfiles.title: Japanese internal economic and political situation
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Schuler)
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a memorandum recording a conversation with former missionary George S. Noss.
subfiles.summary: The referenced conversation concerned Japan’s internal political and economic situation. Noss was identified as a former missionary of the Reformed Church in Japan.

subfiles.title: Japanese internal and foreign policy and economic situation
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram concerning possible Cabinet reorganization arising from dissatisfaction with Japanese policy and economic conditions.
subfiles.summary: The referenced report discussed dissatisfaction with Japan’s internal and foreign policy and its economic situation. It considered the possibility that this discontent could produce a reorganization of the Japanese Cabinet.

subfiles.title: Departmental abstract of despatch no. 5431
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes the Embassy’s assessment of Japan’s New Economic Structure and its proposed economic bodies.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy found little evidence that ambitious plans for a nationally planned economy had been successfully implemented. Industrial opposition forced concessions, notably abandonment of an immediate supreme central control organization, while the adopted plan contemplated government-approved directors, price and dividend controls, and industry-based economic bodies. Because the heavily publicized program could not easily be abandoned, the Embassy expected some implementing gesture but no rapid transformation.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 5431: New Economic Structure
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew analyzes the formulation, compromises, and limited implementation of Japan’s New Economic Structure.
subfiles.summary: The plan arose from wartime shortages and Konoe’s broader New Structure campaign, but industrialists resisted the original restrictions on private management and secured removal of a mandatory supreme control organ. The adopted system envisioned industry-specific economic bodies with government-approved directors, limited state intervention, official control of prices and dividends, and production quotas coordinated across member firms. The principles lacked binding legal force because no implementing Imperial Ordinance had been issued, and only tentative organizational activity was reported in iron, steel, coal, and cement. Grew therefore expected neither rapid nor thorough transformation, although expanded powers under the revised National General Mobilization Law made some implementation likely.

subfiles.title: Complete Text of Principles of the New Economic Structure
subfiles.from: Government of Japan, as published in the Asahi Shimbun
subfiles.about: The opening page states the basic policy for organizing Japan’s national economy within a self-sufficient Greater East Asian defense sphere.
subfiles.summary: The principles seek a coordinated planned economy centered on key industries and based on the combined resources of Japan, Manchukuo, and China. They propose treating capital, management, and labor as an organic unit under a state plan while entrusting day-to-day initiative to industrialists. Public interest, service to the state, national defense, and organization into economic bodies are presented as governing aims.
